synopsis: Fatality patterns differ from collision frequency: heavy-machine contacts are described as the most frequently reported collision type but usually cause property damage, while powered haulage accounted for 13 of 33 US mining deaths (39%) and 426 of 4,792 nonfatal injuries (9%) in 2025 [f11440, f2979, f2980]. For haul trucks, berm and dump-point events dominate deaths: of 54 deaths from 2005 to mid-2021, 21 involved berms, 12 dump points and 13 collisions with people or vehicles; a separate NIOSH review classified 54% of 91 fatal accidents from 2005–2018 as vehicle-environment events [f11404, f5821]. Within the haul-truck collision subset, 12 of 13 deaths involved forward motion, and four began with trucks starting while people were within about 15 m; this should not be generalized to all equipment, since 67% of 22 surface-mine blind-area victims were behind reversing equipment [f11405, f11406, f2986]. Testing should retain known fatal-accident patterns, but vehicle-to-vehicle-focused research and object detection leave the dominant vehicle-environment hazard insufficiently addressed, while automatic braking can itself cause operator injury, load spill, rear-end impacts and rollover [f6639, f6577, f5825, f7456]. On-road precedent illustrates both rare-event validation difficulty and uncertainty in incident evidence: RAND estimated 275 million failure-free miles for a specified fatality-rate demonstration and about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% improvement, while Honda crash and injury totals differ across outlets [f6662, f6663, f1487]. No specific fatality investigation involving failure of a simulation-validated collision avoidance system was found; separately, Tesla PE22-002 closed on 29 June 2026 with no crashes, injuries or defect finding, despite about 25,900 incident reports covering 695,000 vehicles [f7989, f11171, f1501].
